paper.title: LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency
paper.central_claim: LLM+P turns a natural-language planning problem into a PDDL problem file with a GPT-4 one-shot prompt, solves it with a classical planner (Fast Downward), and translates the plan back to natural language; LLM+P is able to provide optimal solutions for most problems while LLMs on their own fail to provide even feasible plans for most problems, and it is demonstrated on a real-robot tidy-up task.
paper.scope_note: Scope flag for Opus: the quantitative evidence is open-loop symbolic planning on seven IPC robot-planning domains; embodiment enters through one qualitative real-robot demonstration (platform not described). Kept in scope as an LLM-plus-solver planning front end for robot task planning (card R01), scored at evidence_level offline; out_of_scope is a defensible alternative reading.

evidence.quote: we find that LLM+P is able to provide optimal solutions for most problems, while LLMs fail to provide even feasible plans for most problems
evidence.support_explanation: Central claim, including 'most problems'.

evidence.quote: However, so far, LLMs cannot reliably solve long-horizon planning problems.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap.

evidence.quote: classical planners, once a problem is given in a formatted way, can use efficient search algorithms to quickly identify correct, or even optimal, plans
evidence.support_explanation: Comparative-advantage rationale for delegation.

evidence.quote: They either use prompting or fine-tuning to make LLMs capable of solving PDDL planning problems.
evidence.support_explanation: Nearest neighbours [47-57] are dismissed in one sentence without naming results.

evidence.quote: However, the SayCan dataset has a limited scope, as it contains only three predefined actions.
evidence.support_explanation: Distinction from the concurrent LLM+PDDL work [66]; comparison is verbal only.

evidence.quote: we assume that for each problem domain, a human expert can provide a domain description (i.e. action preconditions and effects) that will be fixed for all problem instances that happen in that domain.
evidence.support_explanation: Hand-written domain PDDL is an input; the LLM only writes the problem file.

evidence.quote: A simple problem description in natural language and its corresponding problem PDDL file are also provided.
evidence.support_explanation: A human-provided (description, problem PDDL) example is the in-context conditioning.

evidence.quote: A robot knows when to trigger LLM+P based on its conversation with a human user.
evidence.support_explanation: Routing/trigger is assumed, not solved; limitation repeated in Sec I.

evidence.quote: In the end, the LLM translates the PDDL plan back into the natural language to finish up the LLM+P pipeline.
evidence.support_explanation: Back-translation is part of the pipeline but is never evaluated; there is no execution interface description.

evidence.quote: We present seven robot planning domains borrowed from past International Planning Competitions and 20 automatically generated tasks for each domain [ 67 ] .
evidence.support_explanation: Benchmark: 7 public IPC domains x 20 generated tasks = 140 tasks.

evidence.quote: For each problem P , P comes with a natural language description and a ground-truth problem PDDL file.
evidence.support_explanation: Ground-truth PDDL exists; how the NL descriptions were produced (templated or written) is not stated.

evidence.quote: Each domain also includes an example problem description, a corresponding PDDL file, and a plan description, used as context in various approaches.
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline context is an example plan; only LLM+P gets the formal domain file.

evidence.quote: We leverage the gpt-4 model provided by OpenAI for all experiments. We set the temperature to 0 , and use the top probability response.
evidence.support_explanation: Single deterministic GPT-4 run; no variance is possible or reported.

evidence.quote: we feed it into the fast-downward planner and try both aliases seq-opt-fdss-1 (guaranteed optimal) and lama (not guaranteed optimal) with a maximum search time of 200 seconds.
evidence.support_explanation: Solver configuration and the only budget statement.

evidence.quote: For the baseline methods, we manually count the number of optimal plans, and report the number of correct plans in parentheses (if there are any sub-optimal plans).
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline success is hand-counted (no stated plan validator); LLM+P success is whether the planner returns an optimal plan.

evidence.quote: Barman 0 0 0 0 20 (100) Blocksworld 20 15 (30) 0 (5) 0 90 Floortile 0 0 0 0 0 Grippers 25 (60) 35 (50) 10 (20) 0 95 (100) Storage 0 0 (25) 0 0 85 Termes 0 0 0 0 20 Tyreworld 5 15 0 0 10 (90)
evidence.support_explanation: Columns: LLM-as-P without context, LLM-as-P, LLM-as-P (ToT), LLM+P without context, LLM+P (optimal %, correct % in parentheses). LLM+P optimal over 7 domains: 20, 90, 0, 95, 85, 20, 10 (unweighted mean 45.7%); with lama-feasible: 100, 90, 0, 100, 85, 20, 90 (69.3%); LLM-as-P with context: optimal 9.3%, correct 17.1% (our computation from the table).

evidence.quote: The proposed LLM+P produces an optimal plan for the majority of problems.
evidence.support_explanation: Text claim; the table shows optimal plans in under half of the 140 tasks and in only 3 of 7 domains at 85% or more.

evidence.quote: Most failed cases are due to mis-specified problem files, such as missing one of the initial conditions (e.g. leaving the tiles disconnected in Floortile ), causing the planning problem to be unsolvable.
evidence.support_explanation: Failures are in the LLM translation step and are only described, not counted; no repair loop exists.

evidence.quote: Without the context (i.e., an example problem and its corresponding problem PDDL), we observe that LLMs fail to produce correct problem PDDL files.
evidence.support_explanation: Context ablation: LLM+P without context scores 0 in every domain; conditioning is load-bearing.

evidence.quote: In most cases, LLM-as-P fails in the same way with or without the example plan as context.
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline gets the example plan but no formal domain definition: information asymmetry with LLM+P, which receives the expert domain PDDL.

evidence.quote: LLM-as-P (ToT) times out in most cases due to the large number of LLM calls, so it is not suitable for solving long-horizon problems.
evidence.support_explanation: Only cost-related observation: ToT call count and 200 s limit; no times, calls or tokens reported.

evidence.quote: We verify that LLM+P can efficiently solve realistic service robot problems by deploying it on a real robot tasked with tidying up a home.
evidence.support_explanation: Single qualitative robot scenario; robot platform, executor and success are not described.

evidence.quote: LLM-as-P outputs a sub-optimal plan which takes the bottle to the pantry first and travels back for the soup can, with a total cost of 31.
evidence.support_explanation: Demo compares plan costs (22 vs 31) for one problem, not execution outcomes.

evidence.quote: In this paper, we do not ask the LLM to recognize that it has been posed a prompt that is suitable for processing using the proposed LLM+P pipeline.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors' stated limitation on routing.

evidence.quote: We observe that though LLM-as-P provides a plan in natural language for every problem, most of these plans are not feasible.
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline failure mode (cannot reason about preconditions).

signatures.object: Problem-file writer: GPT-4 translates a natural-language problem into a PDDL problem file given a human-written domain and one (description, problem PDDL) example.
signatures.information: Sees the natural-language problem and one worked example; the domain PDDL (predicates, action preconditions/effects) is supplied by a human expert to the planner and is task-agnostic; ground-truth problem PDDL is not shown.
signatures.operation: One-shot in-context translation at temperature 0; single attempt per task.
signatures.output: Problem PDDL file (objects, init, goal, optional metric).
signatures.conditions: Domain file and example exist for each domain; whether to invoke the pipeline is assumed known.
signatures.feedback: none (no planner-failure feedback to the LLM)
signatures.claimed_effect: With context LLM+P solves 90% Blocksworld, 95% Grippers, 85% Storage; without context 0% in all domains.
signatures.failure_boundary: Missing initial conditions (Floortile 0%), hard spatial domains (Termes 20%, Barman 20% optimal), translation errors undetected.

signatures.object: Delegated planning and read-out: Fast Downward solves the generated problem and the LLM re-expresses the plan in natural language.
signatures.information: Planner sees domain file and generated problem file; LLM sees the PDDL plan.
signatures.operation: Run seq-opt-fdss-1 (optimal) or lama (suboptimal) for up to 200 s; back-translate the resulting plan.
signatures.output: Optimal or feasible plan text; for the robot demo an 'optimal tidy-up plan' of cost 22.
signatures.conditions: Time limit 200 s; sound/complete planner returns a plan only if the problem file is consistent.
signatures.selection_rule: not_applicable (optimal alias reported, lama as fallback in parentheses)
signatures.claimed_effect: Plans are optimal when the problem file is correct (soundness of the planner); demo cost 22 vs 31 for LLM-as-P.
signatures.failure_boundary: Planner timeouts; the back-translation step and execution on a robot are not evaluated.

gap.author_gap: LLMs are fluent but cannot reliably produce correct or optimal long-horizon plans; classical planners are sound and complete but need formal input.
gap.checked_gap: Real and supported within the paper: LLM-as-P (with or without an example) is feasible on only about 17% of tasks and optimal on about 9% (our computation from Table I) and ToT times out. The closest competitors (prompting/fine-tuning for PDDL, concurrent [66]) are cited by number only and not compared.
lineage: LLM planners (Huang et al., SayCan, Vemprala et al.) -> LLM + external tools (calculators, ToolFormer) -> concurrent LLM+PDDL on the SayCan dataset [66] -> LLM+P (problem translation + off-the-shelf optimal planner)
gap.closest_adjacent: Concurrent LLM+PDDL work [66] and prompting/fine-tuning works [47-57] are named without results; direct comparison is only against LLM-as-P and Tree-of-Thoughts.
gap.residue: Getting verifiably optimal long-horizon plans from natural-language task descriptions without the LLM doing the search.
gap.stakes: Plan optimality and feasibility on combinatorial robot task domains (plan cost 22 vs 31 in the demo).
gap.method_response: Restrict the LLM to translation into PDDL with a one-shot example and hand the search to a sound planner.
gap.remaining_gap: Human-written domain PDDL and example, translation errors undetected (no repair loop), routing between LLM+P and plain chat left to future work, three domains below 25% optimal, and no closed-loop robot execution evidence.
gap.current_relevance: Not assessed from later work; no later paper in the pinned local set bears on it.
unresolved: Neighbour methods are cited without results, so the lineage position is taken from the paper's text only.

matches.reason: The paper executes the textbook decompose-and-delegate move: the LLM writes a formal artifact and a sound planner computes the plan; it lacks the verification-feedback closure and cost accounting the sub-card emphasises.

matches.reason: The in-context example is an essential, separately demonstrated operation, not just scaffolding, so it is recorded as a supporting match with partial fit.

claims.text: LLM+P gives optimal solutions for most problems, while LLMs alone fail to give even feasible plans for most problems.
claims.setting: Seven IPC robot-planning domains x 20 generated tasks (140), GPT-4 temperature 0, Fast Downward 200 s
claims.baseline_control: LLM-as-P (with and without example), Tree-of-Thoughts, LLM+P without context
claims.selection_vs_test: One example per domain is the context; no stated tuning, no held-out split.
claims.result_denominator: LLM+P optimal 20/90/0/95/85/20/10% (unweighted mean 45.7%), feasible incl. lama 100/90/0/100/85/20/90% (69.3%); LLM-as-P with context optimal 9.3%, correct 17.1% (our computation from Table I)
counterevidence: optimal for under half of the tasks and 3 of 7 domains
baseline lacks the formal domain file
claims.allowed_conclusion: With an expert domain file and a worked example, GPT-4+Fast Downward yields feasible plans on about two thirds and optimal plans on under half of generated tasks, far above direct GPT-4 planning; 'optimal for most problems' is not supported on average.

claims.text: The in-context example is crucial for LLM+P.
claims.result_denominator: 0% in all seven domains without context
claims.allowed_conclusion: A worked (description, problem PDDL) example is necessary for GPT-4 to produce solvable problem files in these domains.

claims.text: LLM+P helps service robots on realistic tasks.
claims.result_denominator: Plan cost 22 (LLM+P) vs 31 (LLM-as-P); no execution trials
claims.allowed_conclusion: For one hand-built problem the generated plan is shorter than the LLM-only plan; no robot execution success is measured.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: Quantitative results score generated symbolic plans/problem files against a planner; there is no closed-loop environment execution, and the robot demonstration is a single qualitative scenario without counts.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: Given an expert-written domain file and one worked example per domain, GPT-4 translation plus Fast Downward returns feasible plans for about 69% and optimal plans for about 46% of 140 generated tasks across seven IPC domains (0% on Floortile), versus about 17% correct for direct GPT-4 planning; the example is indispensable; closed-loop robot performance and 'optimal for most problems' are not shown.
assessment.reproduction: author_report only; our percentages are recomputed from Table I only

G.reason: A clear, important gap (LLM planning unreliability vs sound solvers) with the baseline failure measured on the same benchmark; neighbours (LLM+PDDL prompting/fine-tuning, concurrent [66]) are named only by citation number or one sentence and never compared, so the lineage is incomplete.

M.reason: Translation-not-planning is a well-fitted decomposition: the sound solver guarantees correctness conditional on the problem file, and the example/no-example ablation gives a distinguishable prediction. Weak points: translation correctness is not verified or repaired, and the domain file and example are human-supplied, carrying much of the burden.

X.reason: Pipeline, model, temperature, planner aliases, time limit, assumptions and success definition are stated, so the benchmark runs can be rebuilt. Not 4: provenance of the NL problem descriptions, full per-domain prompts, and the robot execution interface are not in the text; no failure/retry flow.

measurement.reason: Open-loop symbolic scoring with a planner-based criterion for LLM+P but hand-counted baselines without a stated plan validator, 20 tasks per domain (5% granularity), the translated plan never executed, and one qualitative robot demo. Anchor v2: criterion exists but denominators/validator have gaps -> 2.

causality.reason: Same-model comparison with LLM-as-P (with/without example) and ToT, and a no-context ablation, but LLM+P receives the expert domain file while baselines do not, the solver is not separated from that formal information, and only GPT-4 is used.

holdout.reason: One example per domain with no described tuning and no development/evaluation overlap evidence, but all seven domains are public IPC benchmarks whose contamination of GPT-4 is not examined, there is no held-out family, and the robot demo is a single case.

statistics.reason: Single deterministic run per task, no variance or CI; failure causes (missing initial conditions) are described qualitatively and not counted. Anchor v2: no repeats, no failure decomposition -> <=1.

cost.reason: Only a matched 200 s time limit for the planner and ToT and a remark that ToT times out; no planning times, LLM calls, tokens or dollar cost for any method.
